column2: Ghee is my flame in the world, sustaining the life of creatures; I am Ghritarchis, so proclaimed by the steady knowers of the Veda.
Three humours are named, said to be born of action: bile, phlegm and wind; this is called the compound.
By these a creature is sustained and by their decline he declines; therefore knowers of Ayurveda call me Tridhatu.
The blessed Dharma is called Vrisha in the worlds, Bharata; know me, by the word of the Nighantu, as the best Vrisha.
Kapi is the boar, the best, and dharma is called vrisha; therefore the Prajapati Kashyapa calls me Vrishakapi.
Neither the beginning, nor the middle, nor the end do gods and asuras ever know; without beginning, without middle and without end, I am sung as the lord, the pervader, the witness of the world.
I hear pure and hearable things here, Dhananjaya, and I do not take up sinful ones; therefore I am Shuchishravas.
Long ago, becoming a one-horned boar of divine appearance, I lifted up this earth; therefore I am Ekashringa.
So also I was three-humped, taking the boar form; I am famed as Trikakud from the measuring of the body.
He who is called Virinchi by those who contemplate Kapila's knowledge, I am that Prajapati, maker of all worlds by consciousness.
Teachers certain in Sankhya call me Kapila, eternal, dwelling in the sun, joined with knowledge as my companion.
This radiant Hiranyagarbha who is praised in the Veda and always worshipped by yogas, that am I, remembered as the pervader.
They call me the Rig Veda of twenty-one branches, and the Sama of a thousand branches, which knowers of the Veda sing; the brahmins who sing in the Aranyaka are my devotees, and rare.
In the Yajur Veda, whose branches are fifty-eight and thirty-seven, I am remembered in the Adhvaryu office.
The Atharvan of five kalpas, enlarged with magical rites, the brahmins who know the Atharvan also imagine me.
Whatever branch-divisions there are, and the chants in the branches, the pronunciation of accents and letters: know all those made by me.
That Hayashiras, Partha, which arises as the giver of boons, am I, in the northern region, knowing the division of order and letters.
By the path pointed out by Rama, through my grace, the order was gained by the great-souled Panchala from that eternal being; of Babhravya's lineage, he shone, first, master of the order.
Having gained a boon from Narayana and reached the unsurpassed yoga, Galava arranged the order and instruction.
And King Kandalika, the mighty Brahmadatta, remembering again and again the sorrow born of birth and death, attained the wealth of yogas by being chief in seven births.
Long ago I became famed as the son of Dharma, Partha, for another reason, tiger of the Kurus; so I am remembered as Dharmaja.
Nara and Narayana formerly practised imperishable austerity on Mount Gandhamadana, mounted on the vehicle of dharma.
At that very time Daksha's sacrifice took place, and Daksha did not allot a share to Rudra, Bharata.
Then, at Dadhicha's word, Rudra carried off Daksha's sacrifice, and in anger hurled his spear, blazing again and again.
That spear, having reduced Daksha's sacrifice to ash in full, suddenly came to our hermitage at Badari, with great speed, Partha, falling on Narayana's breast.
Then Narayana's hair, filled with his own splendour, became the colour of munja grass, and so I am Munjakeshavan.
And that spear, shaken off by the great soul with a roar, struck by Narayana, went back to Shankara's hand.
Then Rudra ran at those two sages rich in austerity, and Narayana, the self of the universe, seized him as he rushed on by the throat with his hand; hence his blue throat.
Then, to strike Rudra, Nara took up a blade of grass and joined it with mantras, and it became a great axe.
Hurled suddenly at Rudra, it was broken; hence I am remembered as Khandaparashu, from the breaking of the axe.
[Arjuna said:] In that battle, Varshneya, the churning of the three worlds, who gained victory there? Tell me this, Janardana.
[The Blessed One said:] When the two, Rudra and Narayana in nature, were locked in battle, all the worlds were at once alarmed.
Fire did not take the bright oblations well offered at sacrifices, and the Vedas did not shine to the sages of purified selves.
Rajas and tamas entered the gods; the earth shook and the sky split.
The lights lost their brightness, Brahma fell from his seat, the ocean dried and the Himalaya crumbled.
When such a portent arose, son of Pandu, Brahma, surrounded by hosts of gods and great sages, quickly came to the place where the battle went on.
With joined palms, four-faced, knower of the Nirukta, he spoke to Rudra: "May there be good to the worlds; put down your weapons, lord of the universe, for the good of the world.
He who is the imperishable and unmanifest, the lord, the origin of the world, the unchanging, the doer, free of the pairs, whom they know also as the non-doer,
this is his one auspicious form that has come to manifest being; Nara and Narayana, born, lifters of the line of Dharma,
joined with great austerity, best of the gods, of great vows. I am born of his grace for some other reason, and you, dear one, of his anger, eternal in the first creation."
With me, the gods and the great sages, he propitiated the boon-giver, the god Narayana, the lord.
Thus addressed by Brahma, Rudra, letting go his fire of anger, propitiated the god Narayana, the lord, and took refuge in Hari, the primal, choicest boon-giver.
Then the boon-giving god, with anger conquered and senses mastered, was pleased and met Rudra.
Well honoured by the sages, Brahma and the gods, Hari, lord of the world, spoke to the god Ishana:

He who knows you knows me; he who follows you follows me; there is no difference between us; let your mind not be otherwise.
mahabharata:12:330.65	From today let this Shrivatsa be marked on me with your spear, and marked by my hand, you will be Shrikantha.
Having thus produced a mark made by each other, and made unequalled friendship, the two sages with Rudra practised austerity unperturbed, dismissing the dwellers of heaven.
Thus Narayana's victory in battle has been told to you, Partha, and the secret names and their derivations, Bharata, those told here by the sages and recited to you.
In such many forms I move on earth, and in the world of Brahma, and the eternal world of cows, Kaunteya; you were protected by me in battle and gained great victory.
He who goes before you when battle is at hand, know him to be Rudra, Kaunteya, god of gods, the matted-haired.
Time itself is said to be born of anger, I told you; those slain by him earlier were slain by you, enemies.
Bow in restraint to that god of boundless power, the lord of Uma, lord of the universe, Hara, the imperishable.
[Janamejaya said:] Like butter from curds, sandalwood from Malaya, the Aranyaka from the Vedas, and nectar from herbs,
this excellent nectar of a story has been drawn out, Brahmana; you, a storehouse of austerity, have told it, with Narayana as its refuge.
He is indeed the lord, the blessed god, who makes himself the self of all beings. Ah, Narayana's splendour is hard to see, best of the twice-born,
into which at the end of the age all Brahma and the gods, the sages with the gandharvas, and whatever moves or stands enter. I think there is nothing higher or more purifying in heaven or here.
Going to all hermitages and bathing in all sacred fords do not give such fruit as Narayana's story.
We have been wholly purified here by hearing this story from the beginning, which destroys all sins, of Hari, lord of the universe.
It is no wonder that my father Dhananjaya, with Vasudeva as helper, gained the highest victory.
Having reached the great white island and seen the imperishable Hari, Narada, O king, returned and came quickly to Meru, carrying in his heart the burden of what the Supreme Self had said.
Afterwards, O king, he felt great misgiving: "Having gone a long way I have returned here unharmed."
Then he went from Meru to the mountain Gandhamadana and fell swiftly from the sky near the spacious Badari.
There he saw the two ancient gods, best of sages, practising great austerity, devoted to the self, of great vows,
more radiant than the sun that lights all worlds, marked with Shrivatsa, worthy of honour, bearing matted locks,
with webbed hands and feet, marks of the wheel on their feet, broad-chested, long-armed, with four testicles,
with sixty teeth and eight tusks, voices like masses of thunder-cloud, handsome-faced, broad-browed, with fine jaws, brows and noses,
their heads like parasols; thus endowed with marks, called Great Persons.
Seeing them, Narada was glad, was honoured by them, and addressed them with greeting and was asked about his welfare.
He thought within himself, looking intently at the two best of persons: "Those who were in the assembly there, honoured by all beings,
I saw such two best of sages in Shvetadvipa." Thinking so in mind and circling them, he sat down on a lovely seat of kusha grass.
Then those two, dwellings of austerity, glory and splendour, sages endowed with calm and restraint, having done the morning rite,
afterwards, unperturbed, honoured Narada with foot-water and guest-offering, and having done the day's hospitality, sat on their seats, O king.
As they sat there, the place shone like a place of sacrifice with fires blazing with great flames from ghee oblations.
Then Narayana said to Narada, seated at ease, rested, honoured as a guest and comfortable:
Did you now see in Shvetadvipa that blessed, eternal Supreme Self, our supreme nature?
[Narada said:] "I saw the glorious Person, bearing the universal form, the imperishable; there all worlds stood, and the gods with the sages. Even today I see him, seeing you two eternal ones.
The marks with which that Hari, bearing an unmanifest form, is endowed, with those marks you two, bearing a manifest form, are endowed.
I saw you two there at the side of that god, and I have come here today, sent forth by the Supreme Self.
Who in the three worlds could equal him in splendour, glory and fortune, except you two, sons of Dharma?
He told me before the name called Knower of the Field, and the manifestations that will occur and how.
There the men, white, without the five senses, devoted to delight, are all devotees of the Supreme Person.
They always worship the god, and he delights with them; for the blessed Supreme Self is fond of devotees, a lover of brahmanas.
Being worshipped, he always delights, fond of devotees, enjoyer of the universe, all-pervading, kinsman, tender to devotees; he is the doer, the cause and the effect, of great strength and radiance.
Joining himself to austerity, that which is the splendour beyond Shvetadvipa, known as light, shines by its own light.
That is peace in the three worlds for the perfected of purified selves; by this auspicious understanding he stands in the lasting vow.
There the sun does not burn, the moon does not shine, the wind does not blow, while the lord of gods practises hard austerity.
The enjoyer of the universe, standing on the earth on an altar raised from the ground, on one foot, arms raised, facing north, reciting the Vedas with their limbs, practised very hard austerity.
What Brahma, the sages, Pashupati himself, the rest of the best of gods, the Daityas, Danavas and Rakshasas,
nagas, suparnas, gandharvas, siddhas and royal sages constantly offer as oblations to gods and ancestors by rule, all that comes to that god's feet.
All the rites performed by those of single-minded understanding that god himself receives on his head.
No one is dearer to him than the awakened great souls in the three worlds; therefore I went to single-mindedness, and came here, sent forth by the Supreme Self.
Thus the blessed god Hari himself told me; I shall dwell, intent on him, with you two always."
[The Blessed One said:] "The blessed one whose womb is unmanifest, the hard to see Supreme Person: Narada, this word of yours is true.
In the world none is dearer to him than his devotees; therefore the best of the twice-born showed you his own self.
The place of the Supreme Self, who is practising austerity, no one reaches except us two, best of the twice-born.
The radiance that would be of a thousand suns together would be that of his abode, shining by himself.
From that god, lord of the universe, Brahmana, arises forgiveness, best of the forgiving, by which the earth is held.
From that god arises the sap that does good to all beings, by which waters are joined and attain fluidity.
From him arose the splendour whose nature is form and quality, by which the sun is joined and shines on the worlds.
From that god, the Supreme Person, arose touch, by which wind is joined and blows on the worlds.
We two also were born in Dharma's house, best of the twice-born, and resorting to lovely Vishala we took up fierce austerity.
Whatever manifestations of that same god will be dear to the gods and abide in the three worlds, to them, Brahmana, blessings.
We two are joined with our own rule as before, best of the twice-born, having taken up the best vow of all hardships rightly.
You were also seen by us two in Shvetadvipa, ascetic, when you met the blessed one and conversed.
All of it is known to us in the three worlds with moving and unmoving, what will happen or has happened or is, good and bad."
[Vaishampayana said:] Hearing their words, Narada devoted to Narayana engaged in fierce austerity with joined palms.
He muttered duly the many mantras addressed to Narayana for a divine thousand years in the hermitage of Nara and Narayana.
The greatly radiant blessed sage Narada lived there, worshipping that god and those two, Nara and Narayana.
Then the elder, the lord, son of Dharma, said to him: "Whom, best of the twice-born, is worshipped in the rites ordained for gods and ancestors?
Tell me that, best of the wise, as in the tradition, you who have told it: what is this action done, and what fruit is wished for it?"
[Narada said:] "You said before that the rite for the gods is to be done; the deity and the supreme sacrifice is the eternal Supreme Self.
Then, formed by him, I ever worship the imperishable Vaikuntha; and from him came forth Brahma, grandfather of the world.
Pleased, Parameshthi begot my father; I am his first-ordained mind-born son.

I worship the ancestors, good one, when the Narayana rite is done; thus the blessed one himself, father, mother and grandfather, is worshipped by me always at ancestor sacrifices as lord of the world.
There is also another tradition: the ancestors worshipped their sons as gods; the Veda was lost and again taught by sons; then those sons, giving mantras, attained fatherhood.
Surely this was known long ago to you two of purified selves: sons and fathers worshipped each other."

Three are without bodily form and these bearing a form of rice-ball; let them be the ancestors in the world, made by me, eternal.
mahabharata:12:333.19	Father, grandfather and likewise great-grandfather: I alone am to be known here, standing in the three rice-balls.
mahabharata:12:333.20	None is greater than I; whom should I myself worship? Who is my father in the world? I alone am grandfather,
mahabharata:12:333.21	grandfather and father; I alone am the cause here: having said these words, the god of gods, Vrishakapi,
on the boar mountain, Brahmana, having given rice-balls at length and worshipped himself, vanished there itself.
For this reason, wise one, the ancestors called rice-balls constantly receive worship, according to Vrishakapi's word.
Those who worship ancestors, gods, teachers and guests, cows, the best of the twice-born, and the earth their mother, by deed, mind and speech, worship Vishnu alone.
The blessed one dwelling within, in the bodies of all beings, equal in all beings, the lord of pleasure and pain, great, great-souled, the self of all, is heard of as Narayana."

[Vaishampayana said:] Having lived a thousand years in the hermitage of Nara and Narayana, having heard the account of the blessed one and seen the imperishable Hari, Narada quickly went to the Himalaya, where his own hermitage was.
Those two sages Nara and Narayana, famed for austerity, practised excellent austerity in that same lovely hermitage.
Today the lifter of the Pandava line, of boundless prowess, has been purified by hearing this story from the beginning.
Neither the next world nor this is his, best of kings, who by deed, mind or speech hates the imperishable Vishnu.
His ancestors sink in hell for endless years who hates the best of the gods, the god Narayana Hari.
How could the self of anyone be hated? The self, tiger among men, is to be known as Vishnu; so it stands.
This teacher of ours, the sage son of Gandhavati, told this greatness of the Supreme Self; from him I heard this and I have told it to you, sinless one.
Know Krishna Dvaipayana Vyasa to be the lord Narayana. Who else, tiger among men, would be the maker of the Mahabharata, and who would tell the various dharmas except the lord?
He is the womb of the world, the abode of nectar, subtle, ancient, unmoving, supreme; held high by Sankhya-yogis, always known by the self-restrained through understanding.
[Janamejaya said:] In action and in withdrawal, how each is ordained, that we have heard, Brahmana, told by you, sinless one.
And that great Hayashiras you described, of Vishnu the enjoyer of offerings to gods and ancestors, in the ocean first covered with water, that too was seen by the blessed Brahma Parameshthi.
What was that form produced before by Hari, the bearer of the worlds, a form unprecedented, best of the wise, by the great ones' power?
Seeing that best of gods, unprecedented, of boundless might, that holy Hayashiras, what did Brahma do, sage?
This doubt of ours, Brahmana, born of knowledge of the Purana, tell us, wise one, made by the Great Person; we have been purified by you, Brahmana, as you tell the holy story.
[Vaishampayana said:] I shall tell you all the Purana, equal to the Veda, which the blessed Vyasa sang to the king, Dharma's son.
Having heard of the form of the god Hayashiras of Hari's wisdom, the king, a doubt having risen, urged him on.
[Yudhishthira said:] That form which Brahma showed, the god bearing a horse's head: why did that body, made by the god, come about?
The god, joined with knowledge as helper, Vishvaksena Hari, the lord, made his bed in the waters alone, entered into yogic sleep, thinking of creation of the world, varied and born of many qualities.
As he thought of creation, the great quality of the self is remembered; from it ego was born, Brahma the auspicious four-faced, Hiranyagarbha, the blessed, grandfather of all worlds.
In the lotus, born of Aniruddha, then lotus-eyed, radiant, seated on the thousand-petalled lotus, the eternal one.
He saw the world made of water, of wonderful appearance; the lord Parameshthi, standing in sattva, then created hosts of beings.
And before, on a lotus leaf bright as the sun's rays, two drops of water made by Narayana, excellent in quality, existed.
The blessed one, beginningless and endless, unfallen, saw them. One drop there was honey-coloured, of lovely radiance.
That tamasic one became Madhu then, by Narayana's command; the other, hard drop, Kaitabha, was rajasic.
Those two best ones, joined with tamas and rajas, strong, mace in hand, ran following the lotus stalk.
They saw Brahma of boundless radiance seated on the lotus, creating first the four Vedas of lovely form.
Then those two best of asuras, seeing the Vedas embodied, suddenly seized the Vedas as Brahma watched.
Then those two best of danavas, taking the eternal Vedas, quickly entered the nether world in the ocean first covered with water.
When the Vedas were taken, Brahma fell into confusion; then, deprived of the Vedas, he spoke to the lord:

The Vedas are my supreme eye, the Vedas my supreme strength, the Vedas my supreme abode, the Vedas my highest Brahman.
mahabharata:12:335.30	All my Vedas have been taken by force by two danavas; the worlds, deprived of the Vedas, have become dark to me. Without the Vedas what shall I do, set to create the worlds?
mahabharata:12:335.31	Ah, great sorrow born of the loss of the Veda has come upon me; it torments my heart, kindling fierce grief.
mahabharata:12:335.32	Who would raise me, sunk in the ocean of grief, from here today, bring back the lost Vedas? To whom shall I be dear?
While Brahma spoke thus, best of kings, a thought arose in him, best of the wise, to praise Hari; then the lord with joined palms sang the supreme prayer.

Homage to you, heart of Brahman; homage to you, my elder; best of the world's support, treasury of Sankhya and yoga, lord,
mahabharata:12:335.35	maker of the manifest and unmanifest, inconceivable, standing on the path of welfare, enjoyer of the universe, inner self of all beings, unborn,
mahabharata:12:335.36	I am born of your grace, self-born abode of the world; from you came my first mind-born birth, honoured by the twice-born.
mahabharata:12:335.37	My second old birth was from the eye; by your grace my third great birth was from speech.
mahabharata:12:335.38	My fourth birth, lord, was from the ear from you; and my fifth birth, from the nose, is said to be from you.
mahabharata:12:335.39	My sixth birth, from the egg, was made by you, and this seventh birth is lotus-born, of boundless radiance.
mahabharata:12:335.40	In every creation I am your son, free of the three qualities, famed, lotus-eyed one, made of the chief qualities.

mahabharata:12:335.42	Those Vedas of mine are taken; I am blind of eye; wake! Give me eyes; I am dear to you and you are dear to me.
Thus praised, the blessed Person facing every side gave up sleep and, bent on the Veda's work, by lordly power took a second body.
Becoming one with a fine-nosed body, moon-bright, the lord made a white horse's head, the abode of the Vedas.
Its head became heaven with the stars and planets; its long hair became bright as the sun's rays.
Its ear-cavities were the nether worlds, its forehead the earth-bearer; Ganga and Sarasvati, the holy great river, were its brows.
The eyes were the moon and sun, the nose twilight; Om was the refinement, and the lightning-tongue was made.
The teeth, O king, were the ancestors, called Soma-drinkers; the world of cows and the world of Brahma were the lips of the great soul; its neck, O king, was Kalaratri, of the best qualities.
Having made this Hayashiras covered with many forms, the lord of the universe vanished and entered the nether world.
Entered again into the nether world and established in supreme yoga, taking the voice of the phonetic rule, he uttered the sound Om.
Resonant with echo, all-pervading and smooth, it became immersed in the earth, risen with the qualities of all beings.
Then those two asuras, having bound the Vedas by agreement and cast them in the nether world, ran swiftly from where the sound was.
In the meantime, O king, the god bearing Hayashiras, Hari, took all the Vedas gone to the nether world and gave them back to Brahma, and then returned to his own nature.
Having placed Hayashiras in the ocean covered with water, he became the abode of the Vedas, Ashvashiras.
Then the danavas Madhu and Kaitabha, seeing nothing, came back there swiftly; and the place where the Vedas had been cast, as they looked, was empty.
Then, best of the strong, taking the greatest speed, they rose again quickly from the abode of the nether waters and saw that same primal Person, the lord,
white, pure as the moon, established in the body of Aniruddha, of boundless prowess again, entered into yogic sleep,
on a couch of the serpent's coils made by himself, laid above the water and surrounded by garlands of flame,
endowed with spotless sattva, of lovely radiance. Seeing him, the two lords of danavas gave a great laugh.
They, entered by rajas and tamas, said: "This white Person lies asleep.
Surely by him the Vedas were taken from the nether world. Whose is he? Who is this? And why does the blessed one sleep?"
Having spoken these words, they woke Hari; understanding them as wanting battle, the Supreme Person awoke.
Looking at those two lords of asuras, he then set his mind on battle. Then battle took place between them and Narayana.
Both Madhu and Kaitabha, their bodies entered by rajas and tamas, were slain by Madhusudana, as a service to Brahma.
Then, by their quick killing and the recovery of the Vedas, the Supreme Person removed Brahma's grief.
Then Brahma, surrounded and honoured with the Vedas, his enemies slain, created all worlds, moving and unmoving.
Having given the grandfather the foremost understanding for creating the worlds, the god vanished there, back to where Hari had come from.
Having slain those two danavas and made the Hayashiras body, Hari again took that same body for the dharma of action.
Thus the greatly fortunate Hari became Ashvashiras; this ancient lordly boon-giving form has been told.
The brahmana who always hears or bears this, his study will never go to loss.
Having worshipped by fierce austerity the god who bears the head of Hara, the order was gained by Panchala, Rama pointing the way.
This account of Hayashiras, O king, has been told to you, the Purana equal to the Veda, which you asked me.
Whatever body the god wishes to take at any time in the course of his work, he takes it, transforming himself by himself.
This glorious one is the treasury of the Veda, treasury of austerity; he is yoga and Sankhya and supreme Brahman, Hari the pervader.
The Vedas have Narayana as their end, sacrifices are of Narayana's nature, austerity has Narayana as highest, Narayana is the supreme goal.
Sudarshana, delighting in the householder's life, lived with her at Kurukshetra, O king, together with Oghavati.

Blessed one, as I made a resolve long ago, having come to you, ascetic, for the sacrifice, at your word, teacher,
mahabharata:15:7.5	by this touch of your hand, like the touch of nectar, lord, I think I have been revived, lifter of the Kuru line.
With his senses and mind restrained, Krishna lay down, having entered great yoga; then Jara came to that place, a fierce hunter wishing for game.
Neither Savyasachi nor Bhima, nor the twins, bulls among men, nor Karna of true speech, the hero, are fit for hell for long, O king.
